issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette: Mohan, a 64-year-old Indian-American, worked the night shift at a suburban warehouse, moving pallets of manufactured goods under fluorescent lights. A year ago, he was lured to a remote cabin by a former coworker who claimed there were "special training" opportunities for warehouse managers. The stranger promised him a promotion and a hefty bonus. Instead, Mohan was locked in a small, windowless room for six months. Every day, the captor woke him at 3:00 p.m., the same hour that marked the end of Mohan's shift, and forced him to sit on a rickety chair, staring at a coiled snake that slithered along the wall. The snake's hiss, the cold steel of the door, and the flicker of a single bare bulb became the dark hallmarks of his captivity. When the captor finally released him, Mohan found himself alone in a dimly lit warehouse, the night's darkness a relentless reminder of the locked room, and the rattling of the snake's coils echoing in his mind. The repetition of the 3:00 p.m. hour has turned into a trigger that pulls Mohan into a cycle of maladaptive strategies. When the clock strikes that time, he feels an urgent need to stay awake, to lie in the dark and keep his eyes open, as if sleep would surrender him to whatever might be lurking beyond the window. The same hour also sparks a desperate urge for reassurance; he calls his wife, asking repeatedly whether he is "okay," or whether "anything dangerous might be waiting." Whenever he thinks about the snake, the memory of its scales and hiss flares, and he is compelled to check his body for unseen injuries, convinced that some part of him might be damaged. These strategies, in turn, keep the 3:00 p.m. trigger alive: the sleepless vigil and the constant body check reinforce his awareness of the hour's significance, and the more he stays alert, the more the memory of that exact moment is replayed. The darkness that surrounds him during the night triggers a heightened sense of threat: he feels that the night is a period of vulnerability, that danger could strike without warning, and he keeps looking over his shoulder, checking behind him as if someone could slip in. His sense of helplessness-that he cannot stop bad things from happening-feeds this nightly vigilance. The belief that his life is no longer worth living, a grim thought that surfaces whenever he feels the weight of his past, deepens his sense of threat; he interprets every creak and shadow as evidence that the world is hostile. His maladaptive strategies, which were meant to protect him, paradoxically magnify these negative appraisals. The constant reassurance seeking and body monitoring convince him that he is not capable of safeguarding himself, solidifying the idea that life is futile. In turn, these negative appraisals make the night feel even more dangerous, locking Mohan into a loop where the triggers, the strategies, and the threat reinforce one another. For months, Mohan avoided sleep as a survival tactic. He would stay awake until dawn, then check his phone, hoping that his wife's replies would silence the nagging fear that something bad might be happening to him. His wife noticed that he had stopped taking his usual night walk to the store and stopped going to the gym; he was no longer answering calls from friends because he feared being interrupted and reminded of the snake's hiss. He began to think that if he did not keep himself in this hypervigilant state, the world would collapse around him. When he finally went to a therapist, he explained that he was terrified of sleeping in his own bed, of hearing his own breathing as evidence of an unseen threat, and that he could not bear the thought of reliving the event. Mohan's greatest fear now is that the memory will be so vivid at night that he will feel physically ill, that he will lose his sense of self and his life will not feel worth living. He hopes that therapy can help him let go of the nightly rituals that keep the past alive, to find peace in the dark, and to reclaim the hours of the day that once brought him work and purpose.
